exhibits.title: LOCIT
exhibits.category: Engineering · Product Development · Hardware and Software
exhibits.teaser: A smart location-tracking necklace with a companion app for live location and safety alerts.

image.alt: LOCIT companion app on two phones: the teal sign-in screen and a campus map with a location pin.

idea.text: A smart location-tracking necklace paired with a phone app. It tracks GPS location, watches a geofence and monitors temperature.

who.text: Families with young children or elderly relatives who want to locate a loved one in real time, without the wearer needing to carry a phone.

how.text: The necklace uploads sensor data to a web server, which processes and stores it. The app fetches that data to show live location and send boundary, temperature and low-battery alerts.

items.text: Families need an easy way to find young children and elderly relatives in real time. The leading trackers, Apple AirTag and Tile, depend on a phone, which the people LOCIT was meant for often don’t carry.
LOCIT was designed to improve personal safety by tracking the wearer’s location and alerting when they cross a set boundary.
The goal was peace of mind: a lightweight, rechargeable tracker that works on its own, with safe-zone alerts when the wearer wanders too far.
I led a four-person engineering team from design through testing.
I wrote the product requirements document, with measurable targets such as 24-hour battery life and geofencing alert accuracy, and tested the prototype against them.
Scope: GPS tracking, geofencing, sensors and actuators, safety alerts, application development, requirements gathering, team coordination and system testing.
I designed the team’s AZAD logo.
I demoed the system to non-technical audiences.

figures.alt: AZAD team logo: a winged emblem with a power-button icon and a signal-green accent above the word AZAD.
figures.caption: AZAD, the LOCIT team mark I designed.

items.text: The first 3D-printed enclosure was too bulky to wear comfortably as a necklace, so it was reduced in size and iterated until the GPS module, microcontroller and battery fit.
FlutterFlow could not handle the real-time data coming from AWS.
Hard targets for a wearable: under 15 grams, location within 3 feet, updates every 30 seconds, and up to three trackers per phone.

figures.alt: Hand sketch of the LOCIT necklace pendant: a round case on a cord, with the circuit board, wiring and modules drawn inside it in red.
figures.caption: Early concept sketch: what had to fit inside the pendant.

items.text: Market: the PRD cites nearly half a billion smart wearables sold worldwide in 2023 (Statista) and describes a fragmented market led by Apple AirTag and Tile, both of which need a phone.
Form factor: compared a necklace pendant, an armband, a pin or brooch, and a sling bag for comfort, discretion and keeping a camera facing forward. The team chose the pendant.
Moved data handling out of the app and onto a web server: the necklace uploads sensor data, the server processes and stores it, and the app fetches it.
Refined the geofencing algorithms and accuracy thresholds, because GPS accuracy affected how precisely boundary crossings were detected.
Cut scope to fit the prototype: ultraviolet sensors were dropped because of long procurement lead times, Bluetooth was added, and the requirements were revised to match what was built.

Companion app built in FlutterFlow: home, settings and profile pages, a five-icon bottom navigation bar, and a Google Maps widget meant to connect to the necklace’s GPS. The UI was planned in Figma with a site map and a first design draft.
App features: real-time GPS location, geofencing with boundary-crossing notifications, a temperature alert when the device gets too hot, and a battery alert below 20%.
Necklace enclosure designed in Autodesk Fusion 360 and 3D-printed in PLA, with iterations tested for component fit.
Facial recognition was specified as a requirement, designed into the app screens, and worked in the final prototype (confirmed by Victoria, Nov 2026).
items.src: Product requirements document; app design screens

figures.alt: 3D render of the LOCIT pendant enclosure: a smooth, dark, rounded case with a loop for the necklace cord.
figures.caption: Enclosure modeled in Fusion 360.

figures.alt: Hardware block diagram: temperature, UV and vibration sensors, gyroscope and GPS tracker feed a PCB board, along with LEDs and buttons, a camera, a solar panel and battery, microSD storage and a Bluetooth transceiver; the board drives a display.
figures.caption: Planned hardware architecture from the PRD. UV sensors were later dropped.

figures.alt: Three companion app design screens: sign in, geofencing with a Set New Geofence button and previous geofences, and settings for location tracking, geofencing and notifications.
figures.caption: App design screens: sign in, geofencing, settings.

items.text: Tested GPS tracking and geofencing alerts across 20+ scenarios: 98% location accuracy and 100% alert accuracy.
About 20% faster sensor data transfer after replacing the direct AWS integration with a web server, giving faster GPS updates and geofencing alerts.

results.needs: The test data behind these numbers.

items.text: Next steps listed at the time: at least 24 hours of battery life on one charge, thorough testing, UI refinement and user testing. These were plans, not results.
Nice-to-haves left for later: two-way voice with the wearer, a low-battery mode that keeps only location and boundary tracking, and language options.

improve.needs: What Dami would change looking back, in her own words.

story.intro: LOCIT was my senior capstone at Kennesaw State: a GPS necklace and companion app that lets a family see where a loved one is, and get an alert if they leave a safe zone. The name stands for Location Integrated Tracker, and it’s a pun on “locket”, since the tracker is worn as a pendant. I led our four-person team, AZAD, from design through testing.
meta: Python, C, Raspberry Pi, AWS IoT, FlutterFlow, Figma, Fusion 360

sections.label: problem
sections.headline: Tracking that still needs a phone
paras: Families with young kids or elderly relatives want to know where their people are. The trackers everyone knows, Apple AirTag and Tile, depend on a phone, and the people we were designing for often don’t carry one.
So the question became: what would a tracker look like if the wearer didn’t need a phone at all?

sections.label: goal
sections.headline: Light enough to forget you’re wearing it
paras: I wrote the product requirements document with measurable targets, so I could test the prototype against them instead of guessing:
after: It also called for an alert when the battery drops below 20%, and room for up to three trackers on one phone.

sections.label: challenge
sections.headline: Everything had to fit in a pendant
paras: The first 3D-printed enclosure was too bulky to wear as a necklace. I designed the enclosure in Fusion 360, and we kept shrinking and reprinting it until the GPS module, microcontroller and battery fit.
We also had to cut scope. UV sensors came out because the parts took too long to arrive, Bluetooth came in, and the requirements were revised to match what we could actually build.
The full parts list for the prototype came to about $285.

figures.alt: Hand sketch of the LOCIT necklace pendant: a round case on a cord, with the circuit board, wiring and modules drawn inside it in red.
figures.caption: Early concept sketch: what had to fit inside the pendant.

figures.alt: 3D render of the LOCIT pendant enclosure: a smooth, dark, rounded case with a loop for the necklace cord.
figures.caption: Enclosure modeled in Fusion 360.

sections.label: process
sections.headline: Three decisions that shaped it

steps.title: A pendant, not a band
steps.text: We compared an armband, a brooch and a sling bag. The pendant won: discreet, comfortable, and close to where a forward-facing camera would need to sit.

steps.title: Take the data off the app
steps.text: FlutterFlow couldn’t keep up with real-time data coming straight from AWS. I replaced the direct AWS integration with a web server: the necklace uploads, the server stores, the app fetches. Sensor data transfer got about 20% faster, so GPS updates and geofence alerts arrived sooner.

steps.title: Tune the geofence to the GPS
steps.text: GPS accuracy decided how precisely we could catch a boundary crossing, so we refined the geofencing thresholds around it.

after: The companion app, built in FlutterFlow, shows live location, sets safe zones, and sends boundary, temperature and low-battery alerts. A small camera in the pendant runs facial recognition, identifying people the wearer comes into contact with, which gives families more assurance. I also designed our team’s AZAD logo.

figures.alt: Three companion app design screens: sign in, geofencing with a Set New Geofence button and previous geofences, and settings for location tracking, geofencing and notifications.
figures.caption: App design screens: sign in, geofencing, settings.

figures.alt: Prototype hardware laid out on a wooden table: a GPS module with antenna, a USB board, a processor board and a small lithium battery, each labelled.
figures.caption: Prototype hardware: GPS, USB, processor and power

sections.label: impact
sections.headline: What I measured
paras: I tested GPS tracking and geofencing alerts across more than 20 scenarios, then demoed the system to non-technical audiences.
sections.note: These figures come from our own capstone testing, not from use in the field.
after: Field testing also showed the limits. GPS was precise in open areas but drifted on roads with heavy tree cover, and the battery lasted about 2 hours on a full charge, far short of the 24-hour target.

figures.alt: Map with a red GPS track running along roads from north of a lake down toward Marietta.
figures.caption: A GPS track recorded during field testing

sections.label: what I learned
sections.headline: Not every feature is worth building
paras: Our first plan had a lot in it: GPS, a camera, temperature and UV sensors, a solar panel, a display and a speaker. Each one made sense on paper. In practice, every addition brought weight, cost and power draw to something that was meant to be light enough to forget you’re wearing.

The features that mattered were the ones the whole idea depended on: knowing where someone is, and knowing when they’ve left a safe place. When we cut the UV sensors and revised the requirements, the product didn’t get worse. It got clearer.

If I did it again, I’d rank every feature against that core job in the PRD itself, not just set targets for it, and I’d plan the power budget from the first sketch. Our battery lasted about 2 hours against the 24-hour target I’d written, and that gap would decide whether a family keeps using it.

sections.label: what’s next
sections.headline: Where it would go from here
paras: The list we left ourselves: 24-hour battery life on a single charge, more thorough testing, a more polished app, and testing with real families.

idea.text: An AI-powered career assistant for job seekers navigating applications, with a storybook-inspired identity, interactive animation and a wand motif.

how.text: Live AI features analyze a user’s experience against a job description and suggest resume changes, skill-gap guidance and portfolio projects.

problem.needs: The problem job seekers face, in Dami’s words.

items.text: I defined the product requirements and designed the user flows in Figma.

research.needs: Users, user journeys and research done so far.

items.text: Built and deployed live AI features: experience-to-job-description analysis, tailored resume suggestions, skill-gap guidance and portfolio project recommendations.

Further capabilities in the original plan: resume tailoring, job matching, skill-gap identification, learning recommendations, outreach suggestions, recruiter-ready materials, saved resume versions, application metrics and supporting document uploads. None of these is confirmed as built yet.

story.intro: Fairy Job Mother is an AI career assistant I’m building for recent graduates and career changers. It helps people connect the experience they already have to the job they want, with a storybook-inspired look: interactive animation and a magic wand motif.
meta: Figma, Figma Make, live AI integration

sections.label: problem
sections.headline: Experience that doesn’t translate
paras: Recent graduates and career changers often have relevant experience, but struggle to connect it to what a job description is asking for, or to know which projects would prove the skills they’re missing.

sections.label: key decision
sections.headline: It can only use what you give it
paras: The one rule I wouldn’t bend: everything Fairy Job Mother says about you has to come from something you actually shared. If you trained two new coworkers and made a closing checklist, it can help you say that better. It won’t turn it into “increased productivity by 30%” when you never said that.

steps.title: Gaps aren’t failures
steps.text: If a job asks for something your experience doesn’t show, it tells you it isn’t in what you shared, not that you can’t do it.

steps.title: One project, not a reading list
steps.text: Instead of a long list of courses, it picks the gap that matters most and gives you one small project you can actually start.

steps.title: A demo anyone can try
steps.text: Recruiters can click through a made-up example without sharing anything personal, and it still works if the AI is turned off.

sections.label: scope
sections.headline: What I left out on purpose
paras: I kept the first version small on purpose: no job boards, no auto-apply, no accounts, no payments. Every idea had to answer one question: does it make it easier to get from your experience to a clear next step? If not, it waited.
Résumé uploads were one of the things that waited. People started by pasting their experience in, and once the basics worked, I added uploads so you can bring your résumé as it is.

steps.title: Requirements and flows
steps.text: I defined the product requirements and designed the user flows in Figma.

steps.title: A storybook front door
steps.text: I prototyped the landing page in Figma Make as an interactive storybook. Visitors turn the pages, from “It starts with you” to “The next page is yours”, and each spread walks through one step of the idea.

steps.title: Live AI features
steps.text: I built and deployed AI features that compare a user’s experience with a job description, then suggest tailored resume changes, skill-gap guidance and portfolio projects that would demonstrate the right skills. You can paste your experience or upload your résumé.

steps.title: Test, then refine
steps.text: I tested the web app with more than 10 users and refined the recommendations based on their feedback.

figures.alt: An open storybook spread: “Let’s uncover what you bring” on the left page and “Find where you fit” on the right, each above a hand-drawn bouquet of pink and gold flowers.
figures.caption: Turning the page: each spread is one step of the idea

sections.headline: Early signal
sections.note: From a small survey of early testers.

sections.label: what’s next
sections.headline: Still being written
paras: Next, I want to test with more people. After that, maybe saved plans and more career directions, but only if they make the path from your experience to a next step clearer.

exhibits.title: News Corp Product Strategy
exhibits.category: Product Management · User Research · AI Strategy
exhibits.teaser: AI Product Manager Intern, Aug to Oct 2025. How news sites personalize with AI, compared with TikTok and Spotify, and three feature proposals.
exhibits.summary: I studied how news sites personalize with AI compared with TikTok and Spotify, built five audience personas from 500+ survey responses, and proposed three features.

items.text: How well do news sites personalize compared with the social and streaming apps people use every day?

why.needs: Why this mattered to News Corp’s digital teams.

items.text: Analyzed 500+ survey responses and developed five audience personas from reader preferences and trust concerns, then compared content discovery and personalization across four platforms and presented the findings.

NY Post: the homepage shifted from politics to entertainment after a few entertainment clicks, with no obvious preference controls. “Trending Now” and the sidebar followed the last click. No chatbot found.

BBC: shifted more slowly, from politics to science and technology. “My News” exists but has to be found. Related-content boxes reflected browsing. The app’s News Briefs and voice summaries are likely algorithmic.
Comparison: TikTok’s For You page personalizes most strongly, Spotify is strong, and the news sites are far behind. NY Post’s autoplay video and intrusive ads were the biggest friction.

Her reflection: she had not realized how quickly news sites change what they show after a few clicks, and even with AI personalization it felt less personal than social media. (Paraphrased; a direct quote needs the source PDF.)
Recommendations for news: make it feel personal, mix in discovery such as weekly roundups or topic playlists, and think mobile-first with quick, swipeable video.
Proposed three features: personalized feeds, weekly topic roundups and short-form video.
Projected improvements in content relevance and retention. These are recommendations and projections, not shipped outcomes.

results.needs: Survey data and how projections were estimated.

story.intro: As an AI Product Manager Intern at News Corp, I studied how news sites use AI to personalize what readers see, and how that compares with the apps people use every day. Then I turned it into feature recommendations.

sections.label: problem
sections.headline: Why doesn’t news feel personal?
paras: People spend their days in feeds that learn what they like. I wanted to know how well news sites personalize compared with TikTok and Spotify, and what that gap means for readers.

sections.label: research
sections.headline: Readers first, then the products
paras: I started with readers: I analyzed survey responses and built five audience personas from their preferences and trust concerns. Then I tested the products myself.

steps.title: New York Post
steps.text: After a few entertainment clicks, the homepage swung from politics to entertainment, with no obvious way to set preferences. “Trending Now” and the sidebar followed my last click.

steps.title: BBC
steps.text: It shifted more slowly, from politics to science and tech. A “My News” feature exists, but you have to go looking for it.

steps.title: TikTok and Spotify
steps.text: TikTok’s For You page personalizes most strongly, and Spotify is strong too. Both news sites were far behind, and the Post’s autoplay video and intrusive ads were the biggest friction.

after: What surprised me: how quickly a news site changes what it shows after a few clicks, and how it still felt less personal than social media.

sections.label: recommendation
sections.headline: Make news feel like it knows you
paras: I recommended making the experience feel personal, mixing in discovery, and designing mobile-first with quick, swipeable video. That became three feature proposals:

steps.title: Personalized feeds
steps.text: A feed shaped by what each reader actually engages with.

steps.title: Weekly topic roundups
steps.text: Discovery built in, like a playlist for the week’s news.

steps.title: Short-form video
steps.text: Quick, swipeable stories for the way people read on their phones.

sections.note: These were recommendations with projected benefits, not shipped features.
